query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A data-driven machine-learning interatomic potential, trained on multi-temperature phonon and electron scattering data for HfNbTaTiZr with up to ~1 wt.% oxygen, can robustly separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivities and achieve 25–40% better predictive accuracy than previous defect-free or Debye-based methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equimolar HfNbTaTiZr samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and train a specialized machine-learning model that integrates ab initio simulations (with controlled defect configurations) and measured thermal conductivity data at multiple temperatures and oxygen concentrations.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 100–1200 K, with systematically varied oxygen content up to ~1 wt.% in HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic distortions and scattering pathways induced by oxygen impurities influencing both phonon and electronic transport processes.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating real defect-induced scattering effects into a learned interatomic potential, the model isolates phonon versus electron conduction channels more accurately than traditional single-parameter Debye approaches or defect-free DFT simulations, leading to improved agreement with measured conductivities.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict total thermal conductivity within ~25–40% closer to experimentally measured values across intermediate temperatures (200–600 K), maintaining strong accuracy at higher (up to 1200 K) and lower (<200 K) temperatures.
generation.baseline: Prior first-principles or phenomenological conductivity models that cannot fully account for multiple principal elements, oxygen impurity scattering, and the complex atomic-scale environment.
generation.boundary: The approach is specifically tuned for ~1 wt.% oxygen in nominally equimolar HfNbTaTiZr. Predictions for significantly different compositions or impurity levels beyond ~1 wt.% O, or temperatures below 100 K or above 1200 K, remain uncertain without further validation.
generation.uncertainty: Experimentally measured oxygen levels vary and might introduce sample-to-sample discrepancies; the current approach's transferability outside the 100–1200 K range or to different alloy modifications remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a set of HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen concentration (0–1 wt.% in increments), measure thermal conductivity from 100 K to 1200 K, and compare the separate phonon/electron components to the machine-learning model predictions.
measurements: Measure total thermal conductivity using established steady-state or laser flash methods at discrete temperatures (e.g., 100, 200, 300, 600, 900, 1200 K).
Separate lattice and electronic contributions through established electrical resistivity and Seebeck coefficient methodologies, reaching conditions similar to model inputs.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted lattice and electronic contributions deviate from the measured values by more than ~25–40% (beyond known measurement uncertainties) across multiple temperature-oxygen test points, the hypothesis is falsified.

Data Availability Statement

The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . decision.trend: Earlier first-principles simulations (e.g., PMC6093928) used idealized, defect-free representations of high-entropy alloys to estimate temperature-dependent properties, relying on approximations such as Debye temperatures that can become ill-defined for multicomponent alloys. Meanwhile, work on the actual HfNbTaTiZr system (PMC11077685) has focused on synthesis, oxidation behavior, and mechanical performance but has not resolved the separate contributions of phonons and electrons to thermal transport under realistic impurity levels (e.g., ~1 wt.% oxygen). As a result, while computational and experimental tools have advanced, a predictive solution for thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr—one that captures both lattice and electronic contributions in disordered, partially oxygen-doped material—remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: No current method accurately quantifies the split between lattice and electronic heat conduction in HfNbTaTiZr for temperatures spanning below 200 K to above 1200 K under realistic (oxygen-containing) conditions; existing DFT-based or analytical approaches either neglect defects, rely on simplified parameters like single Debye temperatures, or are validated only for idealized samples.
decision.lever: A machine-learning interatomic potential trained on multi-temperature phonon and electron scattering data from both defect-managed ab initio calculations and targeted conductivity measurements of HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen levels (up to ~1 wt.%). The model would be validated on systematically varied oxygen contents and across 100–1200 K.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the current limitations by incorporating real alloy complexity, including defect/impurity scattering, into the learned potential. It should yield predictive thermal conductivity estimates with 25–40% better agreement to experiment, especially at intermediate temperatures (200–600 K) where prior methods deviate most. Decisive tests would compare the predicted separate phonon/electron contributions against carefully measured data at both low (<200 K) and high (~1200 K) temperatures, ensuring the model accurately captures scattering by oxygen, phase variations, and thermal expansion—thus offering demonstrably improved fidelity over traditional Debye-based or purely idealized DFT estimates.
